title: Open work inventory: what's open, what to save, what to drop

steps.path: Every repo, on this computer and on GitHub
steps.headline: What I counted: 140 open cards, 21 closed. About 50 session folders here, about 90 unfinished branches on GitHub, 8 open pull requests.
steps.changed: Five reviewers checked every card and every branch against what is actually in the app today. About 20 of the session folders are finished and simply never removed. About 15 branches were replaced by something newer. About 12 are real unfinished work. A handful of folders hold files never saved anywhere but this disk.
steps.notice: Five sessions are running right now (Android fixes, Pages, the test-suite rethink, mesh sync design, local models). Nothing below touches them. Full findings and the card-to-workstream map: docs/active/investigations/2026-11-08-work-inventory/ on this session's branch.

steps.path: The cards folder and the Work board
steps.headline: The cards are out of date in both directions: shipped work shown as pending, and real progress shown as none.
steps.changed: 14 closed cards still say 'waiting on Destin' or 'nothing shipped', though they shipped. The Android card (#213) says 'Done: nothing yet' while 57 commits of fixes sit on its branch. #172 (Electron upgrade) is already done. #133 (one settings screen for desktop and phone) is obsolete: the phone already shows the desktop's settings. 5 cards name version 1.3.2 as their target, which shipped Oct 21. 55 of 140 open cards have no priority. 28 of 50 work branches aren't linked from any card. The security program merged Nov 1-7 has no card at all.
steps.notice: Two weeks of merged work (security hardening, buddy rebuild, outside-file comments, analytics, voice, the fix for messages that wouldn't send, the freeze fixes) is in the code but in no released version. The last release is 1.3.3 (Oct 23).

steps.intro: Save what's at risk, then clear what's finished. Nothing here changes the app.

steps.path: worktrees/sessions/ (the 148, 163, cc-reliability, 11-direct-controls, persona, user-notify and narrow-screens folders, and three CI bench folders)
steps.headline: Save the never-saved files now, by committing each pile onto its own branch and backing it up to GitHub?
steps.today: Some old work folders hold changes that were never committed. The real work among them: about 1,800 lines of speed-test lab tools (card #148), a half-done fix to what the app says after a crash (card #163), and your answers on an old reliability review deck. The rest is regenerated screenshots and plan drafts that were later rewritten.
steps.problem: They exist only on this disk. A cleanup tool, a disk failure or a mistaken delete would lose them, and no card mentions them.
steps.proposal: Commit each pile onto its own existing branch and push it. That is a backup, not a release. Each pile is then decided on its card.

options.label: Save all piles
pros: Nothing can be lost while you decide.
Costs nothing. Branches can be deleted later.
cons: A few more branches on GitHub until they're cleaned up.

options.label: Only the real work
options.summary: Save the speed lab, the crash-wording fix and your deck answers. Throw away the rest.
pros: Less clutter.
cons: A reviewer judged 'not worth keeping'. It might be wrong.

options.label: Don't save
pros: Nothing new on GitHub.
cons: They stay at risk. The next cleanup could delete them.

steps.path: worktrees/sessions/ and GitHub branches in all five repos
steps.headline: Remove the finished leftovers: about 20 session folders here, and about 16 branches on GitHub whose work is already in the app?
steps.today: About 20 session folders (48 repo copies between them) hold work that's already landed. 4 more folders are empty. About 16 GitHub branches have nothing the app lacks. The automatic cleaner skips the folders because they hold throwaway screenshots and temp files it can't be sure about.
steps.problem: Every session's startup report lists them as warnings, so real problems get buried. They also slow down tools that scan every folder.
steps.proposal: After saving anything from the previous question, delete the finished folders and branches. Before each delete I re-check it holds nothing missing from the app, and I skip anything a running session uses.

options.label: Remove them all
pros: Startup report shrinks to the work that matters.
Each one was checked: everything in it is already in the app.
cons: Old throwaway screenshots in them are gone for good.

options.label: Folders only
options.summary: Remove the folders on this computer but keep their GitHub branches for a month.
pros: A safety net if a check was wrong.
cons: GitHub stays cluttered. Needs a second pass later.

options.label: Leave them
pros: No risk at all.
cons: The clutter keeps growing: about 20 new leftovers in two weeks.

steps.path: Six CI speed experiments (one is pull request #272), release-1-3-2, two old wrap-ups, the 1.3.1 dependency fix, an early copy of the Android branch, an older helper-plans copy, a duplicate of a freeze fix, and the 2-month-old sync-retry pull request #444
steps.headline: Drop about 15 branches whose work was replaced by something newer?
steps.today: Each has commits that aren't in the app, but a later change replaced every one. The CI experiments lost to a different approach that shipped, and their pull requests are already closed. The release-1-3-2 notes were rewritten. The roadmap file two of them edit no longer exists.
steps.problem: They look like unfinished work in every report, so each new session wonders whether to rescue them.
steps.proposal: Delete them, with a one-line note on the card each belongs to saying what was dropped and why. Anything saved under the first question stays until its card decides.
steps.risk: Two calls are medium confidence: the 1.3.1 dependency fix (its files are gone from the app, but I didn't confirm what replaced them) and pull request #272, whose checks pass but whose script no longer exists on master.

options.label: Drop them all
pros: Clears the most confusing leftovers.
Each was checked against what replaced it.
cons: Can't be brought back once deleted from GitHub.

options.label: Keep the two doubtful
pros: Keeps the two medium-confidence calls for a closer look.
cons: Two more leftovers until someone checks them.

steps.path: ~/youcoded-dev itself, and the marketplace's shared copy
steps.headline: Move your personal files out of the YouCoded workspace, archive the Flappy prototype, and throw away stale leftovers?
steps.today: The main folder holds your Anthropic essay (.docx) and 10 'Untitled' Word, Excel and PowerPoint files from Oct 5-23. Six of those are blank; four have content, and one looks like a copy of the essay. Also there: flappy-bird.html, the prototype of the arcade's Flappy game (the game shipped; the prototype has unsaved Sep 11 edits), and 141 MB of old landing-page screenshots whose sources were archived Oct 16. The marketplace's shared copy has 5 edited files that are older drafts of what's already on GitHub.
steps.problem: Personal files in a project folder risk being committed to a public repo by mistake. The stale edits block that shared copy from updating.
steps.proposal: Move the essay and all 10 Untitled files to ~/Documents/youcoded-dev-leftovers (I don't open them). Archive flappy-bird.html with its edits under the workspace's prototypes archive. Delete the old screenshots and the 5 stale marketplace edits.

options.label: Do all of it
pros: Nothing personal can leak into a public repo.
Nothing of yours is deleted, only moved.
The shared copies can update again.
cons: You sort the leftovers folder yourself, or leave it.

options.label: Only move the files
options.summary: Move the personal files, leave everything else as it is.
pros: Smallest change.
cons: The stale screenshots and marketplace edits stay.

steps.path: Dependabot pull requests in four repos
steps.headline: Land the six safe library updates, close the two broken ones, and hand the four big ones to the release workstream?
steps.today: GitHub's bot opened 12 update requests. Six pass every check and change little. Two are stale and failing (a test-tool major version, twice). Four are big jumps that fail Android or app tests, or a version check.
steps.problem: Open update requests pile up and hide security fixes. The big ones can break the Android app if merged carelessly.
steps.proposal: Land the six green ones, close the two dead ones, and make the four big ones one task in the release workstream.

options.label: Yes, as described
pros: Six fewer open items, all passing their checks.
Risky ones get done carefully, not rushed.
cons: Even small updates change what the next release contains.

options.label: All in the release
pros: Every change lands together and is tested once.
cons: They sit open longer.

steps.page: Finished work waiting on your word

steps.path: Several repos

options.label: Four with no app change

pros: Nothing you'll see in the app changes.
Supervisors need that rule, and it's your own decision.
cons: None found.

steps.page: Big unfinished projects that went stale
steps.intro: Three large builds fell 1,700-2,600 changes behind the app. Reviving any of them means rewriting most of it.

steps.path: Card #74 (approve a multi-step job up front), a branch with 140 commits
steps.headline: Helper plans was built but is now very stale. Shelve it with its design record, revive it, or drop it?
steps.today: A full version (the assistant proposes a step-by-step plan you approve before helpers run it) was built in September: 34,000 lines on its own branch. The app moved on 1,705 changes since, and 40 places conflict. Its review deck was never answered. A separate branch holds the only copy of your decision record for it (506 files).
steps.problem: Reviving means days of untangling the chat engine's core, and the design may no longer fit. Leaving it means the card claims more progress than exists.
steps.proposal: Shelve: land the decision record on master as a doc so it's never lost, keep one snapshot branch, delete the other copies, and mark card #74 as exploration with a design reference.

options.label: Shelve with record
pros: Your decisions are safe on master.
No multi-day rebase on a feature nobody is waiting for.
cons: When you want it, it's mostly a rebuild using the old design as a guide.

options.label: Revive it now
pros: Keeps the work already done.
cons: Several days, high risk to the chat engine, and the design must be reviewed again.

options.label: Drop it entirely
pros: Cleanest.
cons: Loses your decision record.

steps.path: Card #75 (choose skills and tools per project), app pull request #571, workspace #203

steps.page: Fix the cards, and stop the drift
steps.intro: So the Work board tells the truth, supervisors start from accurate cards, and this doesn't happen again.

steps.path: cards/ and the Work board
steps.headline: Correct every card that's factually wrong today, in one pass?
steps.today: See the second card on page 1. Shipped work is described as pending, and pending work as not started. Five cards target a release that already happened. Some links point to docs or branches that don't exist. Three cards repeat the same 'chat started' line 26 to 77 times.
steps.problem: You and every agent read these cards to decide what to do next. Wrong cards waste sessions and hide real problems.
steps.proposal: One pass that fixes only facts: rewrites stale progress lines, closes what's truly done (#172), marks #133 obsolete, removes dead release labels, trims repeated lines, fixes dead links, links every live branch to its card, and adds one card recording the security program and its leftovers. Priorities and groupings don't change in this pass.

options.label: Fix the facts
pros: The Work board becomes trustworthy.
Every change has evidence (a commit or pull request) in the findings.
cons: Many cards change at once. Your 'Changed since' view will light up.

options.label: Show me first

steps.path: Priorities on cards

steps.path: How a supervisor session works
steps.headline: Approve this way of running a supervisor?
steps.today: Today one session works one card. Large efforts (security: 12 branches) ended as piles of branches that needed combining before you could review them.
steps.problem: Without a fixed pattern each supervisor invents its own, and you get surprise branches, surprise merges or work that's never reported.
steps.proposal: Each card gets a 'workstream' line and each area a short brief: goal, cards, branches, what done means, what needs you. A supervisor gets its brief, uses one branch per repo with every helper committing onto it, has strong (Opus-class) helpers build and a fresh helper review each piece, backs up to GitHub as it goes, updates its cards as pieces finish, shows you decks only at real decision points, and never lands anything without your word. Its final report names one branch per repo: what's done, what's verified, what needs you.

options.label: Approve as written
pros: Matches your existing rules: no merge without you, one branch per workstream.
One branch per area makes review easy.
cons: Big branches mean bigger reviews. A supervisor can still ask to land a finished part early.

options.label: Land in pieces
options.summary: Same, but the supervisor asks you to land each finished card separately instead of all at the end.
pros: Smaller, more frequent reviews.
Less risk of a giant branch going stale.
cons: More interruptions for you.

steps.path: Which areas start first
steps.headline: Which areas should get a supervisor first?
steps.today: Five sessions already run (Android, Pages, test rethink, mesh sync, local models).
steps.problem: More at once is faster, but supervisors collide when two touch the same files, they use a lot of your plan's usage, and each produces decks for you to answer.
steps.proposal: Start with areas that rarely touch the same code, then add more once the pattern works.

options.label: My three
options.summary: Phone and Android (continuing the running session), Release and tests (gets the security fixes to users), Workspace tooling (makes the rest smoother and stops the drift).
pros: Low collision risk.
A manageable number of decks for you.
cons: Other areas wait a week or so.

options.label: Those plus three more
options.summary: Add Security, Files and Office, and Chat and speed, which are also self-contained.
pros: Much faster across the board.
cons: Higher usage, more collisions, more decks at once.

options.label: One, as a trial
options.summary: Release and tests only, to prove the pattern.
pros: Lowest risk.
cons: Slowest.

steps.path: This session
steps.headline: After you submit, should this session carry out every Yes above, then write the workstream briefs?
